newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says IMF package could be painful.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says IMF package could be painful.

text.p: Thai central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said on Monday an economic austerity package proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) could be painful but the government would try to ease its impact.

"Economic stabilising measures will not always produce only positive results. They could have some impacts. We are tackling domestic problems and will try to minimise the impact," Chaiyawat told reporters.
He did not say how the government would minimise the impact of the austerity measures.
Chaiyawat said the government and IMF officials have reached agreement on key basic points in the package, of which clearer details are expected to be finalised by early next week.

Finance minister Thanong Bidaya told reporters earlier discussions were still going on with the IMF but the basic framework of a package would be presented and was expected to be approved by cabinet on Tuesday.
Thanong would make a nationally-televised address on Tuesday night to explain the package.

Asked how much in loans Thailand would seek from the IMF, Chaiyawat said: "If we managed (to) tackle our problems quickly, we will need less money which will partly include a standby credit that has no negative implication for the country."
The governor said the package was designed to send a signal to the international community that Thailand has moved to boost market confidence and to stabilise its financial sector.
He said talks with IMF officials in the past week had produced very satisfactory results. He did not elaborate.
Neither he nor Thanong commented on reports that Japan would provide loans through the Export-Import Bank of Japan in cooperation with the IMF.
Japanese government sources said on Monday that Tokyo would decide on a financial support package for Thailand within the next two weeks.
The Japanese financial newspaper Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday the Exim bank and the IMF had put togeter an $8 billion emergency loan package for Thailand to boost the economy.
